title: The wounded healer
hook: people who have suffered sometimes become healers, an old idea found in myths and in modern care alike

segments.voice: Yesterday, a warm roll on a bad day. Your line was they are new every morning. Did you find one before sleep? Day seven hundred forty-five.

In Greek myth there's a centaur named Chiron, half man, half horse, who lives in a cave on a mountain and teaches young heroes. He knows herbs, music and medicine. In some tellings he teaches healing to Asclepius, who becomes the god of medicine. And Chiron carries a wound of his own: an arrow, poisoned, that struck him by accident. He is immortal, so he cannot die of it. And it will not heal. The one who teaches healing cannot heal himself. That strange picture has followed people a long way, into churches and clinics. It has a name.
screen: `A CENTAUR WHO TEACHES HEALING.` → `A WOUND THAT WON'T CLOSE.` → `IT HAS A NAME.`

segments.voice: First, the myth. Chiron's wound doesn't stop his work. In the story, it sits right beside it. Much later, the psychiatrist Carl Jung wrote of the wounded physician: the idea that a healer's own hurt can be part of what lets them understand a patient's. Writers after him tied that phrase to Chiron. Second, the letter. Paul, writing to the church at Corinth, puts the same idea in Christian terms. He calls God the one "who comforteth us in all our tribulation, that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble, by the comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted of God." Comfort received becomes comfort passed on. The Catholic priest Henri Nouwen wrote a whole book called The Wounded Healer, about how a minister's own loneliness and pain can become a place where others find welcome. Third, the room down the hall. The idea isn't only old. Some recovery groups are built on it: a person who has been through it, sitting with a person going through it. Some hospitals and clinics bring in peer supporters, people with lived experience of an illness, to sit beside those newly facing it. Nobody has to explain what the first night feels like. Fourth, a caution. Nobody owes their wound to anyone, and some wounds are still too open to lend out. One way to put it: help from a scar, not from a fresh cut. On some days, you are the one who needs the soup. On others, what you came through may be what someone else needs to hear.
screen: `CHIRON: THE HEALER WHO HURTS.` · `COMFORT RECEIVED, COMFORT PASSED ON.` · `SOMEONE WHO HAS BEEN THROUGH IT.` · `FROM A SCAR, NOT A FRESH CUT.` · then, large: `THE WOUND HELPS.`

segments.voice: Settle. Let one hard thing you've come through come to mind, one that has begun to heal, not one still raw. Ask quietly: what did I learn in there that someone else might need? A phone number. A sentence that helped. Something nobody told you at the start. Then let one person come to mind who is near the beginning of something like it. You don't need to reach out now. Just hold them, and what you might offer. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. The bell holds the time.
Chiron, the wounded centaur of Greek myth whose own hurt never closes, and who still teaches healing to others. Today's word.
Your line: the wound helps. Today, if the moment is right, offer one person something you learned the hard way, gently, without a lecture. Day seven hundred forty-five.

howItsDone: Some recovery groups and peer support programs pair people who have come through an illness, addiction or loss with those newly facing it, and some Christians read 2 Corinthians 1:4 as a call to pass on the comfort they have received.

fork.reveal: the wounded healer offers from a scar: one thing that helped, then presence. Paul's word is comfort, passed on, not a lecture.

trapdoor: what you thought: a wounded healer is someone too hurt to help anyone.
what it means: someone whose own suffering, once it has begun to heal, helps them understand and comfort others.

what a scholar hears: Chiron, the immortal centaur with an unhealing wound in Greek myth, linked by later writers to Carl Jung's wounded physician, and taken up by Henri Nouwen in The Wounded Healer; and Paul's comfort passed on in 2 Corinthians 1:4.

notes: Chiron's story varies by source (who wounded him, whether he taught Asclepius); the script says 'in some tellings' and omits Heracles, dates and places. Please confirm the general outline: immortal, wounded by a poisoned arrow by accident, unable to heal.
Jung and Nouwen are paraphrased, never quoted (both under copyright). Please check the paraphrase of Jung's use of the Chiron image.
'Some recovery groups' and 'some hospitals and clinics bring in peer supporters' are general descriptions with no cited source; a reviewer may want a citation or may soften further.
The index hook said 'many who suffered become healers ... myths and hospitals alike'; 'many' softened to 'sometimes' under the claims rule.
The caution paragraph deliberately calls back to day 737 (growth isn't required) so the day does not imply suffering must be made useful.

Audit (2026-10-01): Jung did not himself attach the wounded-physician idea to Chiron as clearly as the draft said ('borrowed Chiron'); the Chiron link is usually credited to later Jungian writers such as Karl Kerényi. Teach, trapdoor and source now say Jung wrote of the wounded physician and later writers tied it to Chiron. Trapdoor no longer says the idea has 'roots in' 2 Corinthians 1:4 (an unsupported lineage claim). 'From a scar, not a fresh cut' is a common modern saying, given as 'one way to put it', not attributed.
